questions.q: State the precise condition that must be satisfied for a set A to be a subset of a set B, using the symbols ∈ and ⇒.
questions.a: A ⊂ B ⇔ (∀x)(x ∈ A ⇒ x ∈ B). A wrong answer like "A ⊂ B means all elements of B are in A" reveals confusion between subset and superset direction. Writing "x ∈ A ∧ x ∈ B" instead of implication shows the student does not grasp the conditional nature of the definition.

questions.q: Let A = {1, 2} and B = {1, 2, 3}. Is A ⊂ B? Is B ⊂ A? Is A a proper subset of B? Justify each answer using the definition.
questions.a: A ⊂ B is true because 1 ∈ A ⇒ 1 ∈ B and 2 ∈ A ⇒ 2 ∈ B. B ⊂ A is false because 3 ∈ B but 3 ∉ A, violating the implication. A is a proper subset of B because A ⊂ B and A ≠ B (3 ∈ B but 3 ∉ A). A student who says "B ⊂ A because B has more elements" confuses cardinality with the subset condition.

questions.q: Given C = {x ∈ ℤ : x² < 10} and D = {−3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3}. Determine whether C ⊂ D and whether D ⊂ C. Show all steps.
questions.a: C = {x ∈ ℤ : x² < 10} = {−3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3} because (−3)²=9<10, (−2)²=4<10, (−1)²=1<10, 0²=0<10, 1²=1<10, 2²=4<10, 3²=9<10, but 4²=16≥10. So C = D exactly. Therefore C ⊂ D (true, every element of C is in D) and D ⊂ C (true, every element of D is in C). Since C = D, neither is a proper subset of the other. A student who writes C = {1,2,3} misses negative integers, revealing they forgot ℤ includes negatives.

questions.q: Consider the statement: "For any sets A, B, C, if A ⊂ B and B ⊂ C, then A ⊂ C." Is this always true? Prove your answer or give a counterexample.
questions.a: Yes, always true. Proof: Assume A ⊂ B and B ⊂ C. Let x ∈ A be arbitrary. Since A ⊂ B, x ∈ A ⇒ x ∈ B. Since B ⊂ C, x ∈ B ⇒ x ∈ C. By transitivity of implication, x ∈ A ⇒ x ∈ C. Since x was arbitrary, ∀x(x ∈ A ⇒ x ∈ C), so A ⊂ C. A student who says "false, counterexample: A={1}, B={1,2}, C={2,3}" fails to check that B ⊂ C is false here (1 ∈ B but 1 ∉ C), revealing they don't verify the premise properly.

questions.q: A student writes: "φ ⊄ {1, 2, 3} because the empty set has no elements, so it cannot be a subset of anything." Evaluate this reasoning and correct the error.
questions.a: The reasoning is incorrect. The definition A ⊂ B means ∀x(x ∈ A ⇒ x ∈ B). For A = φ, there is no x such that x ∈ φ, so the implication "x ∈ φ ⇒ x ∈ B" is vacuously true for every x. Hence φ ⊂ B for every set B, including {1, 2, 3}. The student's error is treating "no elements to check" as "condition fails" instead of "condition holds vacuously." This is a classic logical misunderstanding of universal quantification over an empty domain.

questions.q: Give the correct order of checks that decide whether A subset B and B subset C can deliver A subset C in the example A = {1}, B = {1, 2}, C = {1, 3}.
questions.a: The checks run: (1) Verify A subset B by testing each element of A (2) Test B subset C and find element 2 in B but not in C (3) Conclude the premise of transitivity fails since B subset C is false (4) Note that A subset C still holds here because 1 happens to lie in C, for a different reason. A wrong answer that calls this a contradiction of transitivity shows the student has missed that the law needs both premises, and a false second premise ends the argument.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A set A is a subset of set B, denoted A ⊂ B, if and only if every element of A is also an element of B; ______, A ⊂ B ⇔ (∀x)(x ∈ A ⇒ x ∈ B).
Fill in the blank: Imagine your school has a "Science Club" (set S) and a "______ Team" (set R).
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can determine whether a given set is a subset or proper subset of another by verifying the element-wise implication, can correctly use the symbols ⊂ and ⊄ in statements, and can explain why φ ⊂ A and A ⊂ A hold for any set A.
